questions.prompt: What does “signal flow” describe?
choices: The path a signal takes through a system
How much reverb is on a signal
The kind of cable a signal travels on
questions.explanation: Signal flow is the path audio takes from its source through inputs, processing, routing, and outputs.

questions.prompt: A wireless receiver shows microphone signal, but the mixer input meter shows nothing. What troubleshooting approach best follows signal flow?
choices: Check the cable and routing from the wireless receiver to the mixer input
questions.explanation: Follow the signal in order. The wireless receiver shows signal, so the mic and transmitter are working; the problem is somewhere between the receiver output and the mixer input.

questions.prompt: A DAW is showing no microphone signal. Which should you check first?
choices: Whether the correct input device and track input are selected
Whether the track is panned center
Whether the master fader is at 0 dB
Whether the track has EQ on it
questions.explanation: Correct I/O is fundamental: the DAW must use the intended device and the track must listen to the correct input.

questions.prompt: You want to record through an audio interface, but the DAW is still using the computer’s built-in microphone. What needs to change?
questions.explanation: The DAW records from whichever input device is selected in its audio settings. Choose the interface there, then pick the corresponding input on the track.

questions.prompt: Before recording into a DAW track, what usually needs to be enabled on that track?
questions.explanation: Record-arming tells the DAW which track should receive and record the incoming signal.

questions.prompt: You press Record and the playhead moves, but no new audio appears on your microphone track. What is a likely cause?
choices: The master fader is at 0 dB
questions.explanation: Only record-armed tracks capture new audio. If the track isn’t armed, the DAW runs without recording onto it.

questions.prompt: Which control should you use first to get a healthy microphone level entering a mixer or interface?
questions.explanation: Input gain sets the level entering the channel. Faders are normally used afterward to balance signals in a mix.

questions.prompt: A microphone is extremely quiet at the channel input. Which control is the most direct first adjustment?
questions.explanation: Input gain sets how strongly the mic signal enters the channel. Faders come later, for balancing a signal that’s already healthy.

questions.prompt: In a digital recording system, what is the main problem with reaching or exceeding 0 dBFS?
questions.explanation: 0 dBFS is the digital ceiling. Trying to go beyond it causes clipping.

questions.prompt: You’re doing a test recording before the show, and the input meter hits the red clip light during the loudest passages. What should you do?
choices: Turn down the input gain and test again
Turn down only the main fader
questions.explanation: Since this is a test, fix it now: turn down the input gain and record another test. Don’t wait until the real take to find out.

questions.prompt: You’re recording a live concert and a mic starts clipping just a little on the loudest passages. What should you do?
choices: Pull the gain down just slightly, and note the time and how much you changed it
Leave it alone; fixing clipping in post works fine
Pull the gain down a lot right away to be safe
Stop the recording and restart it
questions.explanation: We prefer not to change gain mid-concert unless it’s really clipping. If you do, change it just a little and log the time and amount, so it can be corrected in post.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest difference between mono and stereo audio?
choices: Mono uses one channel; stereo uses two channels
Mono is quiet; stereo is loud
Mono is analog; stereo is digital
Mono uses XLR; stereo uses USB
questions.explanation: Mono is one channel. Stereo uses two channels, normally left and right.

questions.prompt: You are recording one microphone into Input 1. What track format is usually appropriate?
questions.explanation: One microphone feeding one interface input is a mono source, so a mono DAW track is normally appropriate.

questions.prompt: Which microphone type requires 48V phantom power?
questions.explanation: Condenser mics need 48V phantom power (rare exceptions, like tube mics with their own power supply). Dynamic mics work either way, and ribbon mics must never get it.

questions.prompt: You connect a condenser microphone and the input meter shows nothing. Which setting is worth checking first?
questions.explanation: Condenser microphones need 48V phantom power to work. With it off, you get no signal.

questions.prompt: Which kind of microphone must never be given phantom power?
questions.explanation: Phantom power can damage ribbon mics, so keep 48V off on their channels (rare exception: some modern active ribbons need it). Condensers need it; dynamics don’t care either way.

questions.prompt: What is a basic job of an audio interface?
choices: Connect music hardware — mics, instruments, speakers — to the computer
Automatically mix and master a song
Replace the need for a DAW
questions.explanation: An audio interface connects analog audio sources and outputs with the computer and commonly contains preamps and converters.

questions.prompt: When you record into a computer through an audio interface, where does the microphone plug in?
choices: An XLR input on the interface
questions.explanation: Microphones plug into the interface’s XLR inputs. On many interfaces those are combo jacks that also take a ¼-inch plug.

questions.prompt: A recording call begins at 7:00 p.m. What best matches the course idea of being “on time”?
choices: Send a message at 7:05 saying you are parking
questions.explanation: For recording work, being on time means being ready to work at the scheduled time, not merely arriving at that moment.

questions.prompt: A problem will make you late for a recording call. What best matches the course professionalism standard?
choices: Wait until after the recording to mention it
Only tell another student after the start time
questions.explanation: Reliability includes communicating early, before a scheduling problem becomes a larger problem.

questions.prompt: Your group finishes a camera activity. What best matches “finish the job”?
choices: Restore default settings and return the gear and batteries
Leave as soon as your clips are recorded
Leave the camera on so the next group is ready
Keep the SD card in your bag to check later
questions.explanation: The job isn’t done until the gear is reset and returned. The next person should find it ready to use, with batteries back where they belong.

questions.prompt: Who is the monitor mix primarily for?
questions.explanation: Monitors help performers hear themselves. Their mix can be different from the audience’s Main L/R mix.

questions.prompt: Why might a monitor mix be different from the mains?
choices: Performers may need different things emphasized than the audience does
questions.explanation: Performers often need a custom balance so they can hear what helps them perform, while mains are mixed for the audience.

questions.prompt: A singer asks for more of their own voice on stage without making it louder for the audience. What should you adjust?
questions.explanation: The monitor mix is for the performer and can be adjusted independently from the audience mix.

questions.prompt: What is the basic difference between an active speaker and a passive speaker?
choices: An active speaker has amplification built in; a passive speaker needs an external amplifier
Active speakers use XLR; passive speakers use USB
questions.explanation: Active/powered speakers contain an amplifier. Passive speakers need an external power amplifier.

questions.prompt: You’re setting up a passive speaker. What does it need between the mixer and the speaker?
questions.explanation: A passive speaker has no amplifier inside, so the mixer’s output has to go through a power amplifier first.

questions.prompt: What is the safe basic power rule for speakers?
choices: Speakers ON last and OFF first
Speakers ON first and OFF last
Speakers must stay on all day
questions.explanation: Turning speakers on last and off first helps prevent loud pops and surprises from upstream equipment.

questions.prompt: You are shutting down a live sound system. Which should happen first?
choices: Turn off every microphone before anything else
questions.explanation: Speakers and amplifiers should be turned off first during shutdown to reduce the chance of loud pops.

questions.prompt: What is feedback in a live sound system?
choices: Sound from a speaker re-enters a microphone and loops through the system
A DAW exports a WAV file
A passive speaker receives amplifier power
questions.explanation: Feedback occurs when amplified sound returns to a microphone and is amplified again in a loop.

questions.prompt: A vocal mic starts to squeal whenever the singer walks in front of the main speakers. What’s the best first fix?
choices: Keep the mic behind the speakers and pointed away from them
Turn up the mic’s input gain
questions.explanation: Feedback happens when the speakers’ sound gets back into the mic. Keeping mics behind the speakers and aimed away from them breaks the loop.

questions.prompt: Aperture/iris is primarily a control related to what?
choices: How much light enters through the lens
questions.explanation: Aperture/iris changes the lens opening and therefore affects how much light reaches the camera sensor.

questions.prompt: You change the aperture from F4 to F5.6. What happens?
choices: Less light gets in, because the opening is smaller
More light gets in, because the opening is bigger
questions.explanation: A higher f-number means a smaller lens opening, so F5.6 lets in less light than F4.

questions.prompt: Shutter speed is part of which general camera task?
choices: Controlling exposure and motion rendering (a.k.a. motion blur)
Selecting an XLR cable or 1/4" TRS cable
questions.explanation: Shutter speed affects exposure and also changes how motion is rendered.

questions.prompt: What happens to moving subjects when you use a much slower shutter speed?
choices: They look sharper and more frozen
questions.explanation: A slower shutter exposes each frame for longer, so movement smears into motion blur. The image also gets brighter.

questions.prompt: What is the usual tradeoff when you raise a camera’s gain/ISO?
choices: The image gets brighter but noisier (grainier)
The image gets darker but sharper
questions.explanation: Gain/ISO brightens the image electronically, and that adds visible noise, or grain.

questions.prompt: White balance is mainly used to control what?
questions.explanation: White balance tells the camera how to interpret color under different lighting. Kelvin is commonly used to set color temperature.

questions.prompt: A shot looks unnaturally blue or orange under the room lighting. Which setting is most directly related?
questions.explanation: White balance controls how the camera interprets color under the current lighting.

questions.prompt: What is the simplest purpose of focus?
choices: Make the intended subject appear sharp
questions.explanation: Focus determines what distance/subject appears sharp in the image.

questions.prompt: Which stereo technique uses two directional microphones with capsules very close together and angled apart?
questions.explanation: XY is a coincident stereo technique: the microphone capsules are placed very close together and angled apart.

questions.prompt: Why does an XY recording usually hold up well when it’s summed to mono?
choices: The capsules are nearly in the same spot, so sound reaches both at the same time
questions.explanation: With the capsules together there’s almost no time difference between the two mics, so combining them avoids the phase cancellation a spaced pair can have.

questions.prompt: Which technique is commonly described as a spaced pair of microphones?
questions.explanation: A/B uses two microphones spaced apart to capture stereo information.

questions.prompt: ORTF is best described as which kind of setup?
questions.explanation: ORTF is a near-coincident stereo technique: two cardioid microphones about 17 cm apart, angled 110° from each other.

questions.prompt: In stereo recording, how should the two microphone input gains be set?
choices: Set to matching values unless there is a specific reason not to
One must always be at minimum
The right side must always be louder
questions.explanation: The activity calls for matching gains so the stereo pair begins from a balanced setup.

questions.prompt: For a basic two-channel stereo recording, how are the channels normally panned?
questions.explanation: A basic stereo pair needs distinct left and right channels so the spatial information is preserved.

questions.prompt: Both stereo mic tracks recorded cleanly, but playback sounds like everything is in the middle. What’s the likely setup mistake?
choices: The input gain is too high
questions.explanation: With both channels panned center, the left/right differences collapse into the middle. Pan one hard left and the other hard right.

questions.prompt: In the X32 activity, buses are used for what important task?
questions.explanation: Buses can create separate mixes, such as Monitor 1 and Monitor 2, that differ from the Main L/R mix.

questions.prompt: What does Sends on Fader help you adjust on the X32?
choices: How much of each input is sent to a selected bus
questions.explanation: Sends on Fader lets the faders represent channel send levels into the selected bus, which is useful for monitor mixes.

questions.prompt: What is Dante Controller mainly used for in these activities?
choices: Routing network audio transmitters to receivers
questions.explanation: Dante Controller provides the routing matrix used to connect Dante transmit and receive channels.

questions.prompt: What role does Dante Virtual Soundcard (DVS) play?
choices: It lets a computer send/receive audio channels on the Dante network
questions.explanation: DVS allows computer audio software to use Dante network channels as audio I/O.

questions.prompt: In a Dante routing matrix, what are you creating when you click the intersection between a transmitter channel and receiver channel?
questions.explanation: The matrix intersection connects a transmitting Dante channel to a receiving Dante channel.

questions.prompt: In Dante, what does a transmitter channel do?
questions.explanation: Transmitters send audio onto the Dante network and receivers pick it up. The routing matrix connects a transmitter channel to a receiver channel.

questions.prompt: Why is signal-flow thinking especially useful in a live-looping rig?
choices: Several devices and effects must be connected in the correct order
questions.explanation: A live-looping setup may pass through instruments, effects, a looper, vocal processing, and speakers, so following the signal path is essential.

questions.prompt: In our recording activities, what’s a healthy peak level to aim for?
questions.explanation: Peaks around −12 to −6 dBFS leave headroom for louder moments while staying well above the noise.

questions.prompt: Your test recording peaks around −38 dBFS. What does that tell you?
choices: It’s too quiet; raise the input gain
The track needs to be stereo
questions.explanation: −38 dBFS is far below the −12 to −6 target, so the recording will be noisy once it’s turned up. Raise the input gain and test again.

questions.prompt: Why not record as loud as possible, just under 0 dBFS?
choices: A louder moment in the performance could clip
Louder files take more disk space
questions.explanation: Performances often get louder than the soundcheck, so leave headroom for the loudest moment.

questions.prompt: Which microphone type is rugged and handles loud sources, like guitar amps, especially well?
questions.explanation: Dynamic mics are the tough, loud-source workhorses. Condensers are more sensitive, and ribbons are fragile.

questions.prompt: You’re recording a quiet solo piano recital and want a detailed sound. Which microphone type is the usual choice?
questions.explanation: Condensers are sensitive and detailed, which suits quiet acoustic music.

questions.prompt: Before patching a ribbon microphone into a channel, what should you check?
choices: That the channel is panned hard left
questions.explanation: Phantom power can damage ribbon mics, so make sure 48V is off first (rare exception: some modern active ribbons need it).

questions.prompt: Which connector is the standard for microphone cables?
questions.explanation: XLR is three-pin, locking, and balanced: the standard for microphones.

questions.prompt: What’s the difference between a ¼″ TS plug and a ¼″ TRS plug?
choices: TS has two contacts (tip, sleeve); TRS has three (tip, ring, sleeve)
TS is for speakers only; TRS is for mics only
TS is digital; TRS is analog
questions.explanation: Count the black rings: TS has one, TRS has two. TS carries unbalanced signals like a guitar; TRS carries balanced line signals or stereo headphones.

questions.prompt: An interface input accepts either an XLR plug or a ¼″ plug. What is that input called?
questions.explanation: A combo jack has an XLR socket with a ¼″ hole in the middle, so it takes either kind of plug.

questions.prompt: Which plug is most likely on a pair of laptop earbuds?
questions.explanation: Phones and laptops use the small 3.5 mm (⅛″) plug, usually stereo.

questions.prompt: Your meters look fine. Why record a short test and listen back anyway?
choices: Meters can’t reveal problems like distortion, noise, or the wrong mic
A test raises the sample rate
The DAW won’t record without one
questions.explanation: Meters only show level. Listening back is how you catch distortion, noise, a dead channel, or the wrong mic before the real take.

questions.prompt: When is the best time to test every important input, output, and playback source for a live event?
questions.explanation: Line-check everything before the event. Problems found during the show are much harder, and much more public, to fix.

questions.prompt: What’s the difference between a DAW project and a deliverable?
choices: Project: your editable session. Deliverable: the finished export.
They’re two names for the same file.
Project: the finished export. Deliverable: your editable session.
Project: only the raw WAVs. Deliverable: the DAW file.
questions.explanation: The project keeps everything editable. The deliverable is the finished file someone else receives, like a WAV. Keep both.

questions.prompt: Before you start recording, what should you know about your files?
choices: How long the final mix will be
questions.explanation: Know which folder or drive the project and audio are going to, so nothing gets lost or saved somewhere you can’t find.

questions.prompt: After exporting your mix, why keep the project too?
choices: So you can reopen it and make changes later
The export won’t play without it
It makes the export sound better
questions.explanation: The export is fixed. The project is what lets you go back and change the mix without starting over.

questions.prompt: What does Solo do on a DAW track?
choices: Plays only that track (and any other soloed tracks)
questions.explanation: Solo isolates a track so you can hear it alone. Mute is the one that silences a track.

questions.prompt: You want a finished WAV of your mix to hand in. What do you do?
questions.explanation: Exporting (bouncing or rendering) turns the mix into a finished audio file, like a WAV.

questions.prompt: Which control places a track’s sound between the left and right speakers?
questions.explanation: Pan sets left-right position. Faders set level.

questions.prompt: In a DAW, where do you choose which audio device (like your interface) to record from?
questions.explanation: The input and output device is chosen in the DAW’s audio settings. Each track then picks an input on that device.

questions.prompt: What does the A/D converter in an audio interface do?
choices: Turns the analog signal into digital audio the computer can record
questions.explanation: A/D means analog-to-digital. The D/A converter does the reverse for your speakers or headphones.

questions.prompt: Which order matches basic live-sound signal flow?
questions.explanation: Sound starts at the source, is picked up by the mic, is mixed, is amplified if needed, and comes out of the speakers.

questions.prompt: A recording clipped during the loudest chord. Can you fix it by turning the track down afterward?
choices: No, the distortion is already recorded
Yes, lowering the fader removes it
Yes, exporting as WAV removes it
Yes, panning it center removes it
questions.explanation: Once a signal clips, the distortion is part of the recording. Prevent it with input gain and headroom before you record.

questions.prompt: You have eight tracks and want to record only the vocal. What should be record-armed?
questions.explanation: Arm only the track you mean to record onto, so you don’t record over or add to the others by accident.

questions.prompt: You record with a stereo mic pair. How many input channels does that use?
choices: It depends on the sample rate
questions.explanation: A stereo pair is two mics feeding two inputs: one for left, one for right.

questions.prompt: If you hear an audio engineer say “gain before fader,” what are they probably talking about?
choices: Set a healthy input level first, then use faders to balance
Keep every fader above its gain knob
Raise the faders before touching gain
Gain and faders do the same job
questions.explanation: Input gain gets the signal to a healthy level at the start of the channel. Faders come afterward, for balancing the mix.

questions.prompt: A groupmate is stuck setting up the interface while you wait. What best fits the course’s idea of professionalism?
choices: Help them, or ask how you can help
Wait until they figure it out
Start packing up your own things
Work on something for another class
questions.explanation: Reliability includes helping your group get the whole job done, not just your own part.

questions.prompt: Which three settings make up the exposure triangle?
questions.explanation: Aperture, shutter speed, and ISO/gain together set how bright the image is.

questions.prompt: Why shoot a recital in manual exposure?
choices: So the brightness doesn’t shift on its own during the performance
Manual exposure is required to record audio
Autofocus only works in manual exposure
questions.explanation: In auto, the camera keeps re-guessing brightness as lights and movement change. Manual keeps it where you set it.

questions.prompt: The shot is too dark, and you don’t want more noise or more motion blur. What should you change?
questions.explanation: Raising gain adds noise and slowing the shutter adds blur. Opening the aperture lets in more light without either.

questions.prompt: What does frame rate measure?
choices: How many frames are recorded each second
How many pixels are in each frame
questions.explanation: Frame rate is frames per second (fps), like 24, 30, or 60.

questions.prompt: You’re shooting at 30 fps. Which shutter speed is a common starting point?
questions.explanation: A shutter about twice the frame rate (1/60 at 30 fps) gives natural-looking motion. It’s also what the Cameras activity used.

questions.prompt: You change the shutter from 1/60 to 1/250. What happens to the image?
choices: It gets darker, and motion looks sharper and choppier
It gets brighter, with more motion blur
questions.explanation: A faster shutter lets in less light per frame and freezes motion, which can look choppy in video.

questions.prompt: Which Kelvin setting matches warm indoor (tungsten) light, like the Cameras activity’s default?
questions.explanation: Around 3200 K suits warm indoor light. Around 5600 K suits daylight.

questions.prompt: Why might you switch to manual focus for a fixed recital shot?
choices: Autofocus can hunt or jump to the wrong subject
Manual focus makes the image brighter
questions.explanation: Autofocus may wander when someone walks through the frame or the light changes. Manual focus stays where you set it.

questions.prompt: What does framing refer to?
choices: What’s in the shot and where it sits
questions.explanation: Framing is composition: what the shot includes, and where the performers sit in it.

questions.prompt: Which change brightens the image but adds grain?
questions.explanation: Gain/ISO brightens electronically, and the tradeoff is noise.

questions.prompt: In a system with passive speakers, what comes between the mixer and the speakers?
questions.explanation: Passive speakers have no amplifier inside, so the mixer feeds a power amplifier, which drives the speakers.

questions.prompt: What does a DI box do?
choices: Converts an instrument or line signal into a balanced mic-level signal
Records audio to an SD card
questions.explanation: A DI lets a keyboard, guitar, or playback device connect to a mixer’s mic input over a balanced cable.

questions.prompt: Who normally hears the mains?
choices: Nobody; mains are only for recording
questions.explanation: Mains are the audience mix. Monitors are the performer mix.

questions.prompt: You’re powering up a PA. Which should be turned on last?
questions.explanation: Speakers on last, off first, so pops from other gear powering up never reach them.

questions.prompt: Which change is most likely to reduce feedback?
choices: Point the mic toward the speaker
questions.explanation: Feedback is a loop. Lowering the level, or moving the mic away from the speakers, breaks it.

questions.prompt: Before you raise any levels, what should you know about the mixer’s outputs?
choices: What feeds the mains, the monitors, and the recording
How loud the room can get
questions.explanation: Know where each output goes before turning things up, so nothing surprises the audience, the performers, or the recording.

questions.prompt: Copying the finished recital files to the archive belongs to which core skill area?
questions.explanation: Organizing, backing up, and archiving files is data management & archiving.

questions.prompt: Editing and mixing a recital recording after the concert falls under which core skill area?
questions.explanation: Work done on the recording afterward, like editing and mixing, is post production.

questions.prompt: What are the ORTF spacing and angle?
choices: About 1 m apart, pointing straight ahead
About 17 cm apart, pointing straight ahead
questions.explanation: ORTF uses two cardioid mics about 17 cm apart, angled 110° from each other.

questions.prompt: Compared to XY, the AB stereo mic technique produces:
choices: A wider, more spacious image, but weaker mono compatibility
A narrower image with perfect mono compatibility
It can’t be used for classical music
questions.explanation: Spacing the mics widens the image, but the time differences between them can cause phase problems when summed to mono.

questions.prompt: In XY, how are the two microphones placed?
choices: Capsules as close together as possible, angled apart
One above the stage, one at the back of the hall
questions.explanation: XY is coincident: the capsules sit together and point in different directions.

questions.prompt: Your stereo recording leans left even though the mics are placed symmetrically. What should you check first?
choices: Whether the two input gains match
questions.explanation: If one channel has more input gain than the other, the image pulls toward that side.

questions.prompt: On the X32, what does a bus master fader control?
choices: The overall level of that bus’s mix
questions.explanation: Each channel sends some level into the bus; the bus master sets the level of the whole mix, like one monitor.

questions.prompt: With Sends on Fader active for Bus 1, you raise the vocal channel’s fader. What changes?
choices: How much vocal goes to Bus 1
The vocal level in Main L/R
questions.explanation: In Sends on Fader mode, the channel faders control sends into the selected bus, not the main mix.

questions.prompt: The mains sound fine, but the singer’s monitor wedge is silent. What’s a sensible first check?
choices: The vocal’s send to that monitor bus, and the bus master
questions.explanation: Since the mains work, the input is fine. The problem is in the monitor path: the send into the bus, the bus master, or the bus output.

questions.prompt: How does a wireless mic’s signal get into the mixer?
choices: The mic transmits to its paired receiver, and the receiver’s output connects to a mixer input
The mic sends audio straight to the speakers
The mixer’s 48V powers the wireless link
The mic connects to the mixer over USB
questions.explanation: The transmitter and receiver must be paired; then the receiver’s output is patched into a mixer channel like any other source.

questions.prompt: What does Dante do?
choices: Carries many channels of audio over a computer network
questions.explanation: Dante sends many audio channels over standard network cabling instead of one cable per channel.

questions.prompt: Computer A plays music that Computer B should record over Dante. Which one is the transmitter?
questions.explanation: The device sending the audio is the transmitter. Computer B receives it.

questions.prompt: On a Dante-connected computer, which audio device does the DAW use to reach the network?
questions.explanation: DVS appears to the DAW as an audio device. Dante Controller is the routing software, not an audio device.

questions.prompt: Computer B’s DAW shows no signal from Computer A, and DVS is running on both. What should you check in Dante Controller?
choices: That A’s transmit channels are routed to B’s receive channels
That the network cable is XLR
questions.explanation: Audio only flows on Dante once a transmitter channel is subscribed to a receiver channel in the routing matrix.

questions.prompt: In the looping rig, which device (1) mixes (combines everything), (2) produces sound as a monitor for the performer, and (3) has a single XLR output (mic or line level) to send to the house PA system for the audience?
questions.explanation: The B205D is the mixer and speaker. Every path ends there.

questions.prompt: In the looping rig, which channel is tested last because it’s the most feedback-prone?
questions.explanation: The open headset mic is the one that can feed back, so it’s added last, and it’s the first to turn down if feedback starts.

questions.prompt: Why must the RC-30 and MicroKorg 9V adapters never be swapped?
choices: They have opposite polarity, which can damage the device
Swapping them erases the loop memory
questions.explanation: The Korg adapter is center-positive and the Boss adapter is center-negative. The wrong one can damage the device.

questions.prompt: You hear live guitar, but no loop plays back. Following the rig’s signal path, what should you check?
choices: G3X balanced out → RC-30 mic in, and RC-30 output → Channel 2
questions.explanation: The loop path runs from the G3X balanced output through the RC-30 to Channel 2, so check each link in that path.

questions.prompt: Which of these signals is the very small one that needs a preamp before a mixer can use it well?
choices: The signal from a mixer’s main output
The signal going to a passive speaker
The signal from a powered monitor
questions.explanation: A microphone makes a very small signal. The preamp brings it up to a level the rest of the mixer can work with.

questions.prompt: What kind of signal normally leaves a mixer’s main output and goes to a powered speaker?
choices: There is no signal until the speaker is plugged in
questions.explanation: Line level is the usual mixer-to-powered-device signal. The powered speaker has its own amplifier for the next step.

questions.prompt: A cable has an XLR connector on each end. What does that tell you for certain about the signal it carries?
choices: Nothing for certain, because XLR can carry mic or balanced line signals
questions.explanation: The connector shape doesn’t settle the question. XLR is common for microphones and for balanced line connections, so confirm the signal and the destination before you patch.

questions.prompt: What does a microphone preamp do?
choices: Gives a passive speaker the power to move
Turns a line-level signal into speaker level
Brings a small microphone signal up to a usable level
questions.explanation: The preamp is the early stage that makes a tiny mic signal big enough to work with. It is not what drives a speaker.

questions.prompt: Where does the power to move a passive loudspeaker come from?
questions.explanation: A passive speaker has no amplifier inside. A power amp sits between the mixer’s line output and the speaker and creates the speaker-level power.

questions.prompt: Someone plugs a mixer’s line output directly into a passive speaker. What’s wrong?
choices: Nothing, passive speakers take line level
A power amp is missing: the mixer’s output is line level, not speaker level
The cable should have been XLR
questions.explanation: Don’t connect a mixer line output directly to a passive loudspeaker. The power amp is the part that creates speaker-level power.

questions.prompt: Which description fits a powered studio monitor?
choices: It needs an external power amp
It runs on phantom power from the mixer
It needs AC power and a line input, because the power amp is inside the cabinet
It takes speaker-level signal through a SpeakON cable
questions.explanation: In a powered (active) monitor the power amp lives in the cabinet, so the mixer only has to send it a line-level signal.

questions.prompt: On an analog mixer, which input feeds the microphone preamp?
questions.explanation: The XLR mic inputs feed the microphone preamps. Line inputs accept other source types, such as a keyboard or playback device.

questions.prompt: Along a channel strip, which control comes earliest in the signal path?
questions.explanation: Gain happens early in the channel path. EQ, aux sends, pan, mute, and the fader come along the path after it.

questions.prompt: You walk up to a mixer you’ve never used. Which four things should you find first?
choices: The brand, the model, the year, and the serial number
A mic input, a line/stereo input, a main output, and a monitoring output
The reverb, the compressor, the gate, and the delay
The power switch, the fader, the knob, and the screen
questions.explanation: Mixers look different, but the questions stay the same: where are the inputs, the input gain, the main output, and the monitoring paths?

questions.prompt: Which connector is a locking connector for speaker-level signal between an amplifier and a passive speaker?
questions.explanation: SpeakON is the locking speaker-level connector between a power amp and a passive speaker.

questions.prompt: Which connector is the common stereo playback jack on a laptop or phone?
questions.explanation: A 3.5 mm TRS is the usual laptop or phone stereo playback connection. A mixer input needs the right adapter or cable for it.

questions.prompt: Which statement about connectors and signal types is true?
choices: The same connector, such as XLR or ¼-inch, can carry different signals in different situations
Every ¼-inch connector carries speaker level
RCA connectors only carry microphone signals
questions.explanation: Connector shape is a clue, not an answer. Always confirm what signal is on the cable and what the destination expects.

questions.prompt: Which kind of power comes from a standard U.S. wall outlet?
questions.explanation: Wall power in the United States is typically about 120V AC at 60 Hz.

questions.prompt: Which kind of power does a battery provide?
questions.explanation: Batteries provide DC, and many pieces of audio equipment run on DC.

questions.prompt: What does the power adapter for a piece of audio gear often do?
choices: Converts DC from the wall into AC
Raises the volume of the device
Turns a balanced signal into an unbalanced one
Converts AC from the wall into the DC the device needs
questions.explanation: The adapter takes AC from the wall and gives the device the DC it requires.

questions.prompt: About what voltage and frequency is typical U.S. wall power?
questions.explanation: Typical U.S. wall power is about 120V AC at 60 Hz. The 12V and 48V numbers you see in audio belong to DC supplies and phantom power.

questions.prompt: Which of the 3 conductors in an AC power cable is the safety connection?
questions.explanation: The ground is a safety connection that helps protect people if something goes wrong.

questions.prompt: Which conductor in an AC power cable carries the electrical power?
questions.explanation: Hot carries the power. Neutral is the normal return path, and ground is the safety connection.

questions.prompt: What is the neutral conductor in an AC cable for?
choices: It provides the normal return path
questions.explanation: Hot carries the power out, neutral is the normal way back, and ground is there for safety.

questions.prompt: A rig has an audio hum, and someone suggests snapping off the ground pin on a plug. What should you do?
choices: Never remove or defeat the ground pin to solve an audio problem
Remove it, because it is harmless
Remove it only if the show is about to start
Cover it with tape and plug in anyway
questions.explanation: The ground pin protects people. Find the cause of the hum another way, and ask for help if you can’t.

questions.prompt: A power adapter fits a piece of equipment’s connector perfectly. What should you check before plugging it in?
choices: AC or DC, voltage (same), polarity (same), and amperage (at least same or more)
questions.explanation: Fitting physically does not mean it is safe. Before plugging in: AC or DC, voltage matches, polarity matches, enough amperage, and the connector actually fits.

questions.prompt: A device requires 12V DC, center-positive, 1A. Which adapter is safe to use?
questions.explanation: Voltage and polarity must match exactly, and the amperage must be at least what the device needs. 2A is more than 1A, so it is fine.

questions.prompt: A device says “9V DC, 500 mA, center-negative.” You find an adapter labeled “9V DC, 1A, center-negative.” Can you use it?
choices: No, because the amperage is too high
No, because the amperage must match exactly
Yes, because any 9V adapter will work
Yes: voltage and polarity match and the adapter can provide enough current
questions.explanation: 500 mA is half an amp, so a 1A adapter has plenty. A higher amperage rating is fine; polarity still has to match.

questions.prompt: A device requires 12V DC, 2A, center-positive. Which adapter should you NOT use?
questions.explanation: The adapter has to provide at least the current the device needs. A 1A adapter can’t supply 2A.

questions.prompt: Why is it safe to power a 1A device from a 2A adapter?
choices: The adapter lowers its voltage to match
The device only draws the current it needs; the adapter doesn’t force current into it
The device converts the extra current to sound
It isn’t safe, because amperage must match exactly
questions.explanation: A 2A adapter does not “force” 2 amps into the device. The device draws what it needs. Voltage and polarity are what must match.

questions.prompt: How many amps is 1000 mA?
questions.explanation: 1000 mA = 1 A, so a 500 mA device needs half an amp.

questions.prompt: What is the Zoom F8?
choices: An 8-channel analog mixer with built-in speakers
A portable multitrack recorder with 8 XLR inputs
questions.explanation: The F8 is a portable multitrack recorder: 8 XLR inputs, recording to an SD card.

questions.prompt: Where does the Zoom F8 record its audio?
choices: To the connected computer’s hard drive
questions.explanation: The F8 records to SD cards, which is why the card has to be clean and the files have to be copied off afterward.

questions.prompt: How can the Zoom F8 be powered?
choices: Only 120V AC straight from the wall
questions.explanation: The F8 runs on 8 AA batteries or 12V DC power.

questions.prompt: On the Zoom F8, what does turning a track on do?
questions.explanation: Turning the track on is what record-enables it. Recording starts later, with the record button.

questions.prompt: What does pressing PFL let you do on the F8?
choices: Record a second copy of the channel
Focus on one channel and see its exact gain setting
questions.explanation: PFL lets you focus on a single channel and see its exact gain setting while you check or set the level.

questions.prompt: You plug a condenser mic into an F8 input, but there is no signal. Which step in the channel workflow might be missing?
questions.explanation: The per-microphone steps include turning on +48V phantom power if the mic needs it. Condenser microphones usually do.

questions.prompt: While setting gain on an F8 channel, what are you watching the meter for?
choices: Peaks, so the signal doesn’t clip
questions.explanation: Watch the meter and check for peaks. Then listen on headphones to catch problems a meter doesn’t show.

questions.prompt: What does dual channel recording do on the Zoom F8?
choices: It records two microphones to one track
It doubles the number of XLR inputs
Input 1 also records to Track 5, input 2 to Track 6, and so on up to Track 8
It records video and audio together
questions.explanation: With dual channel recording, inputs 1–4 are also recorded to tracks 5–8, giving each of them a second copy.

questions.prompt: Why record a second copy of a channel at a lower level?
choices: It makes the recording sound wider
It saves space on the SD card
It replaces the need for phantom power
It is a safety track: if the main track clips, the quieter copy may still be usable
questions.explanation: The second track can be recorded at a lower level as a safety. If the main one clips, the quiet copy may still be good.

questions.prompt: With dual channel recording on, the second copy of input 2 lands on which track?
questions.explanation: Input 1 goes to Track 5, input 2 to Track 6, input 3 to Track 7, and input 4 to Track 8.

questions.prompt: Why is “Track 5” not always the same thing as “Input 5”?
choices: With dual channel recording, Track 5 can be the second copy of input 1
The F8 only has four inputs
Track 5 is always reserved for the headphones
questions.explanation: Track 5 is not always Input 5. When dual channel recording is on, tracks 5–8 hold the safety copies of inputs 1–4.

questions.prompt: You pressed record on the F8. “Record is not done.” What should you also verify?
choices: That the front panel is clean
That the batteries are the same brand
The meters are moving, it sounds good in headphones, and the recording actually saved
That the track names are alphabetical
questions.explanation: Always verify: are the meters moving, does it sound good in headphones, and did the recording actually save?

questions.prompt: What does “RECORD ≠ DONE” mean?
choices: Recording is finished when the red light goes out
The F8 can’t record and play at the same time
Pressing record doesn’t mean you’ve captured good audio, so you check it
questions.explanation: A button press isn’t proof. Check that signal is arriving, that it sounds right, and that the file was saved.

questions.prompt: In Final Cut Pro, where does your imported media live?
questions.explanation: The Browser is where imported media lives, the Viewer is where you watch, and the Timeline is where you edit.

questions.prompt: In Final Cut Pro, which area is where you watch the picture?
questions.explanation: The Viewer is where you watch. The Browser holds your media and the Timeline is where you edit.

questions.prompt: In Final Cut Pro, which area is where you edit?
questions.explanation: You edit in the Timeline: cutting at the playhead, trimming, adjusting audio level, and adding fades.

questions.prompt: What do we use Final Cut Pro for in this class?
choices: Copying files to the Backups drive
Combining the video with our better-recorded audio
questions.explanation: Final Cut is the “video side” of post-production: we combine picture with the better-recorded audio.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order for the basic Final Cut workflow?
choices: Import, put clips on the timeline, sync the good audio to the video, trim, fade, check, export
Export, import, sync, trim, fade, check
Fade, trim, import, sync, export, check
Sync, export, import, trim, check, fade
questions.explanation: The basic workflow: set up the Library, import video and audio, put clips on the timeline, sync, trim, add fades, check the result, then export.

questions.prompt: In the Phase 1 pipeline, what does “QC” stand for?
questions.explanation: Phase 1 runs: video plus good audio, sync, trim, fade, QC (quality control), then export H.264 video plus WAV audio.

questions.prompt: When importing media into Final Cut Pro at Chapman, which option should you choose?
questions.explanation: At Chapman we import using File → Import and choose “Leave files in place.”

questions.prompt: What should you export your video as in our workflow?
questions.explanation: We export video as H.264, not ProRes. The audio deliverable is a WAV.

questions.prompt: What resolution do we set the project to for individual movements or clips?
questions.explanation: Set the project to 1080p for individual movements or clips.

questions.prompt: Which Final Cut setting do we turn off in our workflow?
questions.explanation: We disable Background Render as part of our Final Cut setup.

questions.prompt: You trim a clip in Final Cut Pro. What usually happens to your original recording file?
choices: Nothing: it is usually not changed
The original is converted to H.264
questions.explanation: Final Cut is usually not changing your original recordings. It is keeping instructions about how to use them.

questions.prompt: What is Final Cut really building as you edit?
choices: A copy of every file you imported
A backup of the SD card
A new set of microphone recordings
Instructions: “use this part of this file, starting here, ending here, at this level”
questions.explanation: The edit is a set of instructions about which part of which file to use and at what level.

questions.prompt: When does Final Cut Pro create the finished file?
questions.explanation: Then when you export, Final Cut creates the finished file from those instructions.

questions.prompt: Where should you keep your original files organized?
choices: Only inside the Final Cut Library
Outside Final Cut, on the drives
Anywhere, since Final Cut finds them
On the SD card, which you wipe afterward
questions.explanation: Keep your original files organized outside Final Cut. Because we leave files in place, Final Cut points at them.

questions.prompt: What format does a gig folder name follow?
choices: Event name, then the date written out
The card name and the date
questions.explanation: For example, 260914 The Chapman Orchestra: the date as YYMMDD, then the full event name.

questions.prompt: Which gig folder name follows the convention?
questions.explanation: The gig folder uses the full event name after YYMMDD. Short names (such as WS) go on the folders inside it.

questions.prompt: Inside a gig folder, where do the files copied from the capture media go?
choices: In the “r” folder, in a folder named From plus the card name
questions.explanation: Source material goes in the r (raw) subfolder, with one “From …” folder per card or SSD.

questions.prompt: What do the r, e, and s subfolders in a gig folder stand for?
choices: Raw, edit, and saved final deliverables
questions.explanation: r is raw/source files, e is edit/post-production files, and s is saved final deliverables.

questions.prompt: You exported the finished video. Which subfolder holds saved final deliverables?
questions.explanation: The s folder is where finished deliverables are saved.

questions.prompt: Which statement about r, e, and s is correct?
choices: They are three backup copies of each gig
They are the three drives used at a gig
They stand for three different cameras
They are stages and file types, not three backup copies of the same folder
questions.explanation: The r/e/s folders describe stages and file types. A matching safe copy of the whole gig folder lives on the Backups drive.

questions.prompt: What is the optional “a” subfolder for?
questions.explanation: An optional “a” subfolder can hold special “archival” files.

questions.prompt: You have a card full of recordings from a gig. Where should a beginner copy everything?
choices: To both the Post drive and the Backups drive
questions.explanation: The beginner default is to copy everything from the capture media to a Post drive and a Backups drive: one source, two destinations.

questions.prompt: Why copy to two drives?
choices: Two drives copy twice as fast
The card needs to be wiped
A hard drive can fail at any time, so one copy is not enough
A single drive can’t hold a gig folder
questions.explanation: A hard drive can fail at any time — one copy is not enough.

questions.prompt: As a beginner, how much of the card should you copy?
choices: Only the files you think you need
questions.explanation: Copy everything by default. Experienced engineers may copy selectively, but only when they truly know what they are doing.

questions.prompt: A card is named Mus128_1842. What does the “128” mean?
choices: The number of files on it
questions.explanation: In Mus128_####, 128 is the card capacity and #### is the unique ID that matches the Data Volumes spreadsheet.

questions.prompt: A gig has several cards. How is each one copied into the gig folder?
choices: All mixed together into one folder
Into its own “From [card name]” folder inside r, on both drives
Only the biggest card is copied
Into the e folder on the Post drive only
questions.explanation: Each source gets its own From … folder inside the r folder, on both the Post and Backups drives.

questions.prompt: When is it okay to delete files from the original card?
choices: As soon as the copy finishes on one drive
Whenever the card is nearly full
Only when you can prove it exists safely in all three places
Whenever a classmate says it’s fine
questions.explanation: The three places are the original card or SSD, the copy on the Post drive, and the copy on the Backups drive.

questions.prompt: Which three things make up the “Triple Triple Check”?
choices: The file name, the color, and the date
The card brand, the drive brand, and the cable
The size in pages, the length in minutes, and the volume
The approximate GB, the last 3 digits of the exact bytes, and the locations all match
questions.explanation: Check the approximate GB matches, the last 3 digits of the exact bytes match, and the files are in the expected source plus the two drives.

questions.prompt: You are about 99% sure everything copied correctly. What should you do?
choices: Do not delete, and ask for help
Delete the originals, since 99% is enough
Delete half now and half later
Reformat the card to be safe
questions.explanation: If you are 99% sure, do not delete. Ask for help.

questions.prompt: The checks all pass. What’s the next step to free the card?
choices: Move the files to the Trash, empty the Trash, and confirm the free space
Copy the files a third time
questions.explanation: Trash then Empty Trash, then confirm free space. Delete only when you can prove the source exists safely in all three places.

questions.prompt: You moved files to the Trash on a card. Are they deleted?
choices: Yes, the space is free right away
Yes, but only on the card
No: trashed is not deleted until the Trash is emptied
No, they are on the Backups drive
questions.explanation: “Trashed” is not deleted. The space doesn’t come back until the Trash is emptied.

questions.prompt: A 128 GB card shows only 106 GB available after you “deleted” everything. What’s the most likely cause?
choices: The card is a 106 GB card
questions.explanation: The files are still in the Trash, so the space isn’t available yet.

questions.prompt: After the Trash is emptied with the card still connected, about how much space should show as free on a 128 GB card?
questions.explanation: It will probably show about 127 GB free or so. Older cards lose some maximum capacity.

questions.prompt: You arrive for a gig and find SD cards that still need cleaning from the last one. What do you do?
choices: Finish that leftover business first, before your own setup
Start your setup and get to it later
Wipe the cards without checking them
questions.explanation: Check for unfinished business from the last gig. If there is something left over, finish it first.

questions.prompt: You’re going to be late for a gig. What should you do?
choices: Wait and see if anyone notices
Skip the gig without telling anyone
Text your fellow engineers before your call time
questions.explanation: Don’t leave your teammates wondering. Text them before your call time.

questions.prompt: For recording work, “on time” usually means:
choices: Walking in at the scheduled time
Arriving a few minutes after the start
Being there by the end of sound check
Ready to work at the scheduled time
questions.explanation: On time usually means ready to work at the scheduled time, not walking in at that time.

questions.prompt: At Salmon, what should you do about the audio preamps?
choices: Don’t adjust them; if a level is wrong, talk to Borecki
Turn them all up for safety
questions.explanation: If a level is genuinely wrong, that’s a conversation with Borecki, not a knob you turn.

questions.prompt: How do you power the Zoom F8 on or off?
choices: Hold the power switch for about 2 seconds
questions.explanation: The F8’s power switch needs about 2 seconds held down to turn on or off. A quick tap does nothing, in either direction.

questions.prompt: When the F8 is set up for a gig, how many channels should show a red record-enable light?
choices: Only the channels with a mic
questions.explanation: All 8 channels should show a red light underneath. If one isn’t lit, press that channel’s button to record-enable it.

questions.prompt: You check both audio recorders with headphones. What should you hear?
choices: The same signal on both, doubled
A clean signal on both, not the same signal doubled
questions.explanation: Confirm clean signal on both the F8 and the H6, not the same signal doubled.

questions.prompt: When do you start recording for a gig?
questions.explanation: Start recording 3 minutes before the downbeat, so nothing is missed.

questions.prompt: At the end of the show, which button stops the F8?
choices: The power switch, with a quick tap
questions.explanation: On the F8 it is the STOP button, not the red record button.

questions.prompt: After pressing record on every device, what must you confirm?
choices: Every device is the same brand
Every recorder is actually rolling: numbers moving, not just a button pressed
questions.explanation: Confirm every recorder is actually rolling — numbers moving, not just a button pressed.

questions.prompt: What is the default for intermission?
questions.explanation: Don’t pause as a matter of course. It’s simpler and safer to record straight through.

questions.prompt: At intermission a device is low on space. What do you do?
choices: Stop all recording devices together, fix it, and restart them all together right away
Let it run out during the show
questions.explanation: If anything is genuinely at risk, stop all recording devices together, fix it, and restart all of them together, immediately.

questions.prompt: Before you go into the green room, what do you do?
questions.explanation: Knock first. Don’t just walk in.

questions.prompt: A performer is already in the green room and you need the TV on. What do you do?
choices: Turn it on quickly without asking
Leave and don’t set it up
Ask before touching anything, and offer to turn it on and show where the volume is
questions.explanation: If a performer is inside, ask before touching anything: offer to turn on the TV and show them where the volume is.

questions.prompt: Once doors open, what do you do on the CRESTRON for the hallway?
choices: Switch the TV to Signage and turn audio off
Switch the Hallway TV from Signage to Camera and turn Hallway Audio on
questions.explanation: At doors, the Hallway TV goes from Signage to Camera and Hallway Audio goes on. At end of show it goes back to Signage with audio off.

questions.prompt: After a gig, at what point do you text Borecki about drive space?
choices: If either the Post or the Backups drive has less than 1 TB free
Only if both drives are completely full
If you are curious how much is left
questions.explanation: If either drive has less than 1 TB free, text Borecki. It’s an actual text, not a “should I ask.”

questions.prompt: Before you copy anything from the cards, what do you do?
choices: Copy first and make folders afterward
Create all of the destination folders on both drives first
Make the folders on one drive only
questions.explanation: Create all of the destination folders first, on both drives, before you copy anything.

questions.prompt: Which drives do you use for the transfer?
choices: Any drive that is plugged in
The ones whose labels you read, because the numbers roll forward over time
questions.explanation: Read the label, don’t assume it’s still whatever was written in an older set of instructions.

questions.prompt: Before any card is wiped, who looks over the transferred files?
choices: Nobody, the Triple Triple Check is enough
questions.explanation: Get Borecki to look over the transferred files before anything gets deleted.

questions.prompt: After wiping a card, how do you confirm it actually worked?
choices: Get Info (⌘I) on the card and check the free space is close to its full size
Look at whether the card is warm
Check that the card’s name changed
questions.explanation: Get Info on each card you just cleaned. The free space should be close to the card’s full rated size.

questions.prompt: What does an aux send do?
choices: Sends the channel to the audience only
Sends some of a channel to another mix, such as a monitor mix
Adds phantom power to the channel
questions.explanation: An aux send takes some of a channel and sends it to another mix.

questions.prompt: A drummer wants more vocal in their monitor, without the audience hearing more vocal. What do you adjust?
questions.explanation: Each channel can send a different amount to the aux, so the monitor changes while Main L/R stays the same.

questions.prompt: A performer likes their monitor balance but everything in it is too quiet. What do you raise?
choices: The aux master or output level
questions.explanation: The aux master changes the whole monitor mix. Raising every send would change things you don’t need to.

questions.prompt: A singer says “more of my voice” in the monitor. What do you raise?
choices: The aux send on the singer’s channel
The preamp gain on every channel
questions.explanation: “More of me” is one source inside the monitor mix, so raise that channel’s aux send.

questions.prompt: What does a pre-fader send do?
choices: Taps the signal after the fader
Taps the signal before the channel fader, so moving the fader doesn’t change the send
Sends the signal to the audience
questions.explanation: A pre-fader send stays the same when front-of-house moves the channel fader. It’s useful for performer monitors.

questions.prompt: A singer’s monitor send is pre-fader. The audience says the vocal is too loud, so you lower the vocal fader. What happens in the singer’s monitor?
questions.explanation: With a pre-fader send, lowering the channel fader changes Main L/R but not the monitor. That is why monitor mixes often use pre-fader sends.

questions.prompt: Which kind of send follows the channel fader, and is useful for effects?
questions.explanation: A post-fader send follows the channel fader.

questions.prompt: Can you assume every aux on every mixer is set up the same way?
choices: Yes, aux sends are always pre-fader
Yes, aux sends are always post-fader
Yes, they are labeled the same on every mixer
questions.explanation: Do not assume every aux is configured the same way. Check the mixer.

questions.prompt: What does PFL stand for?
questions.explanation: PFL is pre-fader listen. AFL is after-fader listen, and some mixers call it Solo or Cue.

questions.prompt: What is the basic purpose of PFL, Solo, or Cue?
choices: To listen to or meter a signal without necessarily sending it to the audience
questions.explanation: The labels vary, but the purpose stays the same: listen to or meter a signal without necessarily sending it to the audience.

questions.prompt: When is PFL most useful?
choices: For setup and troubleshooting, before turning up the room
questions.explanation: Use it for setup and troubleshooting before turning up the room.

questions.prompt: Who is the Main L/R mix for?
questions.explanation: Main L/R usually feeds the audience system. The main mix answers: what should the audience hear?

questions.prompt: An aux send is only an internal mix until...
questions.explanation: A bus is an internal mix path. The output connector is where that path physically leaves the mixer.

questions.prompt: What level of signal leaves an aux output?
questions.explanation: The aux output from the mixer is still line level, so a passive monitor needs a power amp.

questions.prompt: Which path correctly feeds a passive monitor wedge from Aux 1?
choices: Aux 1 bus, then the monitor directly
Main L/R, then the power amp, then the preamp
The preamp, then the aux bus, then the microphone
Aux 1 bus, then Aux 1 output, then a power amp, then the passive monitor
questions.explanation: Aux 1 bus → Aux 1 output → power amp → passive monitor. For a powered monitor, the power amp step is already inside the cabinet.

questions.prompt: What is a bus on a mixer?
questions.explanation: A bus is an internal mix path. An output connector is where that path physically leaves the mixer.

questions.prompt: You go from F4.0 at 1/60 to F5.6 at 1/30. What happens to the overall brightness?
choices: About the same: you lost one stop and gained one back
There is no way to tell
questions.explanation: F4.0 to F5.6 is one stop less light, and 1/60 to 1/30 is one stop more. They cancel.

questions.prompt: You compare F4.0 at 1/60 with F5.6 at 1/30. Both are about equally bright. What else is different?
choices: The second has less depth of field and less motion blur
The second has a different color cast
The second has more depth of field and more motion blur
questions.explanation: Same exposure, different picture. A smaller opening gives more depth of field, and a slower shutter gives more motion blur.

questions.prompt: The hall is bright and the picture is overexposed. You want to keep the same motion blur and the same noise. Which control do you change?
questions.explanation: Shutter speed controls motion blur and gain controls noise, so the iris is the control left to take light away.

questions.prompt: Which exposure control changes both brightness and depth of field?
questions.explanation: Aperture affects brightness and depth of field. Shutter speed affects brightness and motion blur. ISO or gain affects brightness and noise.

questions.prompt: The hall is dark and the iris is already wide open. Which fixes are left, and what does each cost?
choices: Closing the iris, which costs nothing
A slower shutter (more motion blur) or more gain/ISO (more noise)
Changing white balance, which costs focus
A faster shutter, which costs noise
questions.explanation: Once the iris is wide open, brightness has to come from the shutter or from gain. Each one trades something away.

questions.prompt: Which of these apertures lets in the most light?
questions.explanation: A lower f-number is a bigger opening. F2.8 is the biggest of these, and F11 the smallest.

questions.prompt: You change the aperture from F8 to F5.6. What happens?
questions.explanation: Going down one step on the f-number scale (…2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11…) lets in one stop more light.

questions.prompt: On the f-number scale 2.8, 4, 5.6, 8, 11, what does each step toward the higher number do to the light?
choices: Halves it: one stop less per step
Leaves it the same but changes color
Halves it, but only for the shutter
questions.explanation: Each step on that scale is one stop. Moving to the higher number cuts the light in half.

questions.prompt: You change the shutter from 1/60 to 1/30. How much more light reaches the sensor?
choices: None, shutter speed only affects blur
questions.explanation: Doubling the exposure time doubles the light, which is one stop. Shutter is the control you change by doubling or halving the time.

questions.prompt: Which is the faster shutter speed, 1/60 or 1/250?
questions.explanation: 1/250 of a second is a shorter exposure than 1/60. Faster means less light and less motion blur.

questions.prompt: Compared with 1/60, a much faster shutter like 1/250 gives…
choices: A brighter image with more blur
A darker image with each moment looking crisper
questions.explanation: A shorter exposure lets in less light and freezes motion more. You’d use it when you want crisp action and have light to spare.

questions.prompt: You go from ISO 400 to ISO 1600. How many stops brighter is that?
questions.explanation: Each doubling of ISO is one stop: 400 to 800 is one, and 800 to 1600 is two.

questions.prompt: On a camera that shows gain in dB, how many dB is one stop?
questions.explanation: It is 6 dB per stop, not 3 dB. Gain in dB is measured on the amplitude scale, where a doubling is 6 dB.

questions.prompt: What is the cost of raising ISO or gain to brighten a dark shot?
choices: More visible noise, especially in the dark parts of the picture
questions.explanation: Gain brightens the picture electronically, and that brings up noise too.

questions.prompt: In photography and video, what is a “stop” of light?
choices: A doubling or halving of the light reaching the sensor
questions.explanation: Every exposure control is measured in stops, which is why an engineer can say “give me a stop more” to someone holding a camera they’ve never touched.

questions.prompt: Your shot is one stop too dark and you’ll fix it with gain alone. You are at 3 dB. What do you set?
questions.explanation: One stop is 6 dB, so 3 dB plus 6 dB is 9 dB.

questions.prompt: Going from ISO 400 to ISO 800 is how much of a change in light?
questions.explanation: ISO doubling is one stop. That is the quick way to remember it.

questions.prompt: Raising gain from 3 dB to 15 dB is how many stops?
questions.explanation: 15 minus 3 is 12 dB, and 12 dB at 6 dB per stop is two stops.

questions.prompt: F4.0 to F5.6 is…
questions.explanation: F4.0 to F5.6 is one step along the f-number scale, which is one stop less light.

questions.prompt: Is 3 dB on one camera the same as ISO 400 on another?
choices: Not as a rule: those are house numbers for particular cameras. What transfers is the stop (+6 dB or ISO ×2)
Yes, as long as the cameras are the same brand
No, because dB is for audio only
questions.explanation: A camera at 0 dB is at its own base sensitivity, which differs by body. Don’t convert between the two units; think in stops.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a way to give a shot “a stop more” light?
choices: Opening the iris one step, such as F5.6 to F4
Changing the white balance from 3200 K to 5000 K
Doubling the exposure time, such as 1/60 to 1/30
questions.explanation: White balance changes the color cast. It does not change how much light hits the sensor.

questions.prompt: What is depth of field?
choices: How much of the scene, from near to far, appears acceptably sharp
How much noise is in the picture
questions.explanation: A deep depth of field keeps both near and far things sharp. A shallow one keeps only a thin slice sharp.

questions.prompt: You want more of the scene in focus, from the near object to the far one. Which aperture change helps?
choices: Opening the iris, such as F8 to F4
Closing the iris, such as F4 to F8
questions.explanation: A smaller opening gives more depth of field. Going from F4.0 to F5.6 makes the picture darker with more of the scene in focus.

questions.prompt: A wide-open iris (a low f-number) tends to give…
choices: More light and a shallower depth of field
Less light and a deeper depth of field
questions.explanation: The bigger the opening, the more light, and the less of the scene stays in focus.

questions.prompt: You close the iris for more depth of field in a dim room, and the picture gets too dark. What can you do to brighten it?
choices: Raise the gain or slow the shutter, accepting more noise or more motion blur
questions.explanation: Brightness has to come from somewhere. Gain costs noise, and a slower shutter costs motion blur.

questions.prompt: What is the house default in the Portable Cameras activity?
choices: F4.0, 3 dB (ISO 400 on the GH5), 1/60, 3200 K, autofocus
questions.explanation: The house default is the known baseline: F4.0 · 3 dB (ISO 400 on the GH5) · 1/60 · 3200 K · autofocus.

questions.prompt: When do you set a camera to the house default in the Cameras activity?
choices: Never, you leave it as you found it
At the start, and again before the camera goes back in the cabinet
questions.explanation: You set it twice: once to start from a known baseline, and once so the next person finds it that way.

questions.prompt: A camera comes out of the cabinet in whatever state the last person left it. What do you do before recording?
choices: Set it to a known baseline and confirm all five values on the display
Start recording and fix it afterward
Leave it, because the last person set it up
questions.explanation: Nobody is going to walk you through the menus. Set the five values and read them off the screen before you record.

questions.prompt: After you record your first clip, what should you do before shooting the others?
choices: Keep shooting and check at the end
Pull the SD card, open the file on a computer, and confirm it plays and has audio
questions.explanation: Do not shoot the other clips before you know the card is actually recording. Students lose whole sessions this way.

questions.prompt: When comparing what a setting does, why change only one setting at a time and keep the framing identical?
choices: Otherwise you can’t tell what caused the difference
The camera can only store one setting
questions.explanation: If the framing, the light, or two settings changed, the comparison is worthless.

questions.prompt: The camera says the SD card is full, locked, or missing. What should you NOT do?
choices: Check that the card is seated
Find a different card or ask
questions.explanation: Do not reformat. Check the card is seated and the slider is up, then find a different card or ask.

questions.prompt: In the Cameras activity, what is a “slate”?
choices: Reading your settings aloud on camera
questions.explanation: Reading the settings out loud on camera records which values each clip used, so you can match clips to settings later.

questions.prompt: What does an ND (neutral density) filter do?
choices: Reduces the light reaching the sensor without changing the color
questions.explanation: Neutral means it dims the picture without tinting it.

questions.prompt: It’s bright daylight. You want a wide-open iris and 1/60 shutter, but the shot is overexposed. What helps?
questions.explanation: The ND filter takes light away so you can keep the aperture and shutter speed you actually want.

questions.prompt: Why use an ND filter instead of just closing the iris?
choices: An ND filter makes the shot sharper
ND filters change the white balance for you
Closing the iris would change your depth of field, and an ND filter doesn’t
questions.explanation: With ND you can keep the depth of field and motion blur you chose and still control brightness.

questions.prompt: It’s a dark recital hall. Will an ND filter help you get a brighter picture?
choices: No, an ND filter only removes light
Only if the shutter is slow
questions.explanation: ND filters are for too much light. In a dark hall you need the opposite.

questions.prompt: An ND filter cuts the light by 3 stops. What fraction of the light gets through?
questions.explanation: Each stop halves the light, so three stops is one half times one half times one half, which is one eighth.

questions.prompt: Focal length, in millimeters, mainly describes what about a lens?
choices: How much light it lets in
How wide or narrow (zoomed in) a view it gives
How close the subject must be
questions.explanation: A shorter focal length gives a wider view. A longer one is more zoomed in.

questions.prompt: You zoom in to fill the frame with a soloist. What changed?
choices: The focal length got longer, so the field of view is narrower
questions.explanation: Zooming in raises the focal length and narrows what the camera sees.

questions.prompt: Which of these focal lengths gives the widest view?
questions.explanation: The shorter the focal length, the wider the view.

questions.prompt: You need to fit a whole ensemble in the shot, and you can’t move the camera back. What helps?
questions.explanation: Zooming out gives a wider view. At a recital, wide framing also leaves room for performers when they bow.

questions.prompt: What is focus distance?
choices: How far the camera can zoom
How much of the scene is sharp
The distance from the camera to the thing that is in sharp focus
questions.explanation: It’s where the lens is set to be sharp. Depth of field is how far the sharp zone extends from there.

questions.prompt: A camera is on manual focus, set on a singer. The singer walks well forward. What happens?
choices: They stay sharp, because focus follows people
They go soft, because they’re no longer at the distance the lens is set to
questions.explanation: In manual focus the focus distance stays where you left it, so check focus whenever the subject moves.

questions.prompt: You refocus from a near object to a far one. What did you change?
questions.explanation: Refocusing changes the distance the lens is sharp at. Focal length is how wide the view is.

questions.prompt: What does “AoIP” stand for?
questions.explanation: Dante is audio over IP: multichannel digital audio over a network.

questions.prompt: What can a single Ethernet cable do on a Dante network?
choices: Carry many channels of audio, replacing a thick analog snake
Carry audio but never at full quality
questions.explanation: Instead of a thick analog snake with oodles of cables, there is one Ethernet cable.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Dante Virtual Soundcard (DVS) is true?
choices: It only works with one DAW
It’s licensed software that makes your computer appear as an audio interface in a DAW’s I/O
questions.explanation: Any DAW (Logic, Ableton, Reaper) can use DVS if it’s installed. Choose the correct audio I/O in the DAW.

questions.prompt: In Dante, what do TX and RX stand for?
questions.explanation: TX is transmit and RX is receive.

questions.prompt: Dante Controller “does not make sound.” What does it do?
choices: It plays audio over the network
It creates the subscription between transmit and receive channels, like a virtual patch bay across the network
questions.explanation: It is the routing tool: it decides where network audio goes. The sound itself comes from the DAW through DVS.

questions.prompt: Where do you choose which audio interface a DAW uses?
choices: In the Dante routing matrix only
In the DAW’s audio I/O settings
questions.explanation: DAW I/O is where you choose the audio interface. Dante Controller chooses where network audio goes.

questions.prompt: Which tool chooses which transmit channel feeds which receive channel on the network?
questions.explanation: Dante Controller creates the subscriptions. It does not choose the DAW’s device.

questions.prompt: To send audio from a DAW out over Dante, what should the DAW’s output device be set to?
choices: Whatever the other computer is using
questions.explanation: The transmitting DAW’s output has to go to DVS, or nothing reaches the network.

questions.prompt: On the receiving computer, how do you hear and record the incoming Dante audio?
choices: Set the DAW’s input to Dante Virtual Soundcard, make a track with input Dante 1–2, and turn on input monitoring
Set the output to Dante Virtual Soundcard
Nothing is needed once routing is green
questions.explanation: The receiving track needs its input set to the right Dante channels, and input monitoring on so you can hear it.

questions.prompt: Dante Controller shows green routing, but a classmate hears nothing. What’s the most likely next thing to check?
choices: Whether their DAW’s input device is actually set to Dante Virtual Soundcard
questions.explanation: Green routing means the network connection exists. The DAW still has to be listening to DVS.

questions.prompt: To send a stereo signal from one computer to another, which routes do you make in Dante Controller?
choices: Only transmit ch. 1 to receive ch. 1
Transmit ch. 1 to receive ch. 2 only
No routes: DVS does it automatically
Transmit ch. 1 to receive ch. 1, and transmit ch. 2 to receive ch. 2
questions.explanation: Stereo is two channels, so both must be routed.

questions.prompt: You hear sound in only one ear when you expected stereo. What’s the most likely cause?
choices: The track is mono instead of stereo, or only one Dante channel got routed
Dante Controller needs to be reinstalled
questions.explanation: Check that the source is actually stereo and that both Dante channels 1 and 2 are routed.

questions.prompt: In Dante Controller, what should the routing squares look like once a route is made?
questions.explanation: Green means connected. Gray or red means something isn’t.

questions.prompt: How do you tell your computer from others in Dante Controller?
choices: By its IP address written on the monitor
By the color of the squares
By its Local Hostname (the iMac number), typed into the Filter boxes
questions.explanation: Note the Local Hostname in System Settings, then use Filter Transmitters and Filter Receivers to find it.

questions.prompt: Why build a Multi-Output Device on the transmitting computer in a Dante computer to computer situation?
choices: To receive audio from the network
So it can send audio over Dante and still hear it locally
questions.explanation: The Multi-Output Device combines Dante Virtual Soundcard with your local headphone output.

questions.prompt: If you’re connecting two computers with Dante and you want the transmitter to be able to “hear itself”, you’ll open Audio MIDI Setup. After building a Multi-Output Device, what should the DAW’s output be set to?
questions.explanation: The Multi-Output Device is what sends to both places at once.

questions.prompt: In Audio MIDI Setup, in a Multi-Output Device, what determines each device’s channel numbering?
choices: The order you check the boxes
Every device always starts at channel 1
questions.explanation: Channel numbering follows the order of the checked boxes.

questions.prompt: When you build a Multi-Output Device, which box do you check first?
questions.explanation: Check the DVS box before the local interface, or your channel numbering will come out different than expected.

questions.prompt: Three computers each send a stereo source to one receiving computer. Which channel map avoids collisions?
choices: It doesn’t matter, Dante mixes them
Transmitter 1 to channels 1–2, transmitter 2 to 3–4, transmitter 3 to 5–6
questions.explanation: Each source needs its own receive channel pair so each lands on its own track.

questions.prompt: Why does each transmitter need its own receive channel pair?
choices: So each source arrives on a separate track instead of overriding another
Dante limits the whole network to 2 channels
questions.explanation: Dante doesn’t mix two sources into one destination.

questions.prompt: You route a second source to a channel pair that’s already in use. What happens?
choices: The new route silently overrides the first one: Dante doesn’t mix them
Dante refuses and shows an error
questions.explanation: Dante never lets two sources share one destination. The first source just stops arriving.

questions.prompt: In Dante: You only hear Transmitter 2, and Transmitter 1 should also be playing. What’s the most likely cause?
choices: The receiving computer needs more RAM
Both were routed to the same receive channel pair, so Transmitter 2 overrode Transmitter 1
DVS supports only one transmitter at a time
questions.explanation: Look at the full routing matrix, not just your own row.

questions.prompt: In the Dante Jam Session, which computer acts as the “mixer” of the multiple software instruments on other computers?
choices: The receiving computer, whose output would feed the room’s speakers
questions.explanation: Everyone’s audio routes into one computer that acts as the mixer. That computer’s output is what feeds the room.

questions.prompt: How is the Dante Jam Session different from Dante Broadcast?
choices: In the jam, many senders go to one receiver; in Broadcast, one computer sends to one or more computers
Broadcast uses many senders and one receiver
questions.explanation: Broadcast is one computer to one or more computers. The jam session is many senders into one receiver.

questions.prompt: The receiving computer hears nothing. What do you check first in Dante Controller?
choices: Whether the computer is plugged into AC
Whether the routing squares are green or gray/red
The color of the Ethernet cable
questions.explanation: Start with the network connection. Then check the DAWs’ DVS settings, input monitoring, and the headphones.

questions.prompt: Dante Controller shows a red square in the lower right, such as “Clock: No clock source found.” What does it mean?
choices: A network-wide clock problem: a master clock source needs to be set and active
questions.explanation: This is a network-wide problem, not just your computer. Flag it to your instructor if you can’t resolve it.

questions.prompt: In OH B01, which device must you NOT re-route or disconnect in Dante Controller?
choices: Any other iMac in the room
The receiving computer in a jam session
The one labeled INST, the instructor computer feeding the room’s main speakers
questions.explanation: Breaking INST cuts the sound for the whole room, including other classes.

questions.prompt: In the DAW to X32 example, what connects the DAW DVS transmit channels to the X32’s receive channels?
choices: A subscription made in Dante Controller
questions.explanation: DAW to DVS to the Dante network, then Dante Controller subscribes transmit to receive, and the X32 Dante card receives.

questions.prompt: Multitrack DAW outputs 1–8 are sent over Dante to an X32 with a correctly configured Dante expansion card installed. What does each output end up as?
choices: Its own channel on the X32, on its own fader
questions.explanation: If the routing works, each stem lands on its own X32 fader.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct signal path for sending DAW audio to another computer over Dante?
choices: DAW, then the network, then the other computer’s speakers directly
DVS, then the DAW, then Dante Controller, then the network
DAW, then DVS, then the network, then DVS, then the other DAW, then its output
Network, then DAW, then DVS, then Dante Controller
questions.explanation: The activities’ diagram: source to DAW to DVS to network to DVS to DAW to output.
